text: Lesson 17 ended on exactly this problem: sometimes the external system your business depends on has no official ServiceNow spoke. A niche internal inventory system, a homegrown billing platform, a regional vendor's API — none of these ship a Slack-style bundle of ready-made actions. IntegrationHub's answer isn't falling back to a Script step every time. It's: use the custom Action builder to create your own action, once, and let every other flow builder reuse it the way they'd reuse an official spoke's action, without ever knowing the target system's API exists.

Every custom action has the same three parts, in order. First, Inputs — named parameters other flow builders will supply; you define each one's name, type, and whether it's required. Second, an internal step sequence — the actual work, defined once inside the action, usually a single REST step calling the target API, though an action can chain more steps if needed. Third, Outputs — named results read back, mapped from the response, exposing only the fields a consumer needs.

This is the detail that separates using IntegrationHub from building on it. Course 4's generic REST step lived directly on a single flow's canvas, configured once, used once. The REST step inside a custom action is configured once, inside the action definition, and the action itself — not the raw REST step — gets reused across every flow that needs it. A flow builder consuming your custom action never sees a REST step, an endpoint, or an Authentication Profile; they see Inputs and Outputs, exactly like with any official spoke action. You've effectively authored your own mini-spoke.

The internal REST step still authenticates against the target system the same way any REST call in this course has: by referencing an Authentication Profile set up back in Chapter 3. You configure that reference once, inside the action, and every flow that later uses your action inherits correct, centrally-managed authentication without a flow builder ever touching a credential.

A custom action becomes part of what other teams rely on, so before calling it done, confirm three things: the Inputs are named clearly enough that someone who's never seen the target API can guess what to supply; the Outputs expose only what a consumer needs, not every raw field the API returned; and the Authentication Profile is meant for shared, ongoing use, not a personal token that breaks when you leave the project. Next up: a worked lab putting this pattern into practice.
